fields.rationale: States cluster around whether they cap days-of-supply (short hard limits), restrict dosage in MME, require physician involvement or oversight, prohibit dispensing certain schedules outright, set layered rules with named exceptions, or focus on consultation/referral thresholds.

assignments.raw_value: Initial prescription for opioid may not exceed seven-day supply to adult patient for outpatient use; may not exceed seven-day supply to minor. Exceptions allowed for acute medical condition, chronic pain management, pain associated with cancer, palliative care, or logistical/travel barriers with documentation.
Five-day period or less for opioid prescriptions

Registered nurse practitioners, clinical nurse specialists and certified nurse midwives are prohibited from dispensing schedule II controlled substances that are opioids, except for implantable devices or opioids for medication-assisted treatment for substance use disorders

Initial prescriptions limited to seven-day supply for opioid-naive patients; may include second fill for seven-day supply. Exceptions for chronic pain, cancer pain, post-surgical pain, and palliative/hospice care.

The formulary must also limit the prescribing of Schedule II controlled substances as listed in s. 893.03 to a 7-day supply, except that such restriction does not apply to controlled substances that are psychiatric medications prescribed by psychiatric nurses.

prescribing Schedule II narcotic drugs, such as opioids, only in a consultation relationship with a physician; the specific Schedule II narcotic drug may be administered by oral dosage or topical or transdermal application; delivery by injection or other route of administration is not permitted; at least monthly, the advanced practice registered nurse and the physician must discuss the condition of any patients for whom an opioid is prescribed
Schedule II controlled substances limited to 72-hour supply without refill; hydrocodone combination products limited to 30-day supply without refill
Lowest effective dose; quantity no greater than needed for expected duration of pain, except for substance-related disorders, cancer pain, end-of-life/hospice/palliative care, or chronic pain

Prescribers may not exceed 100 MME/day; no more than 30-day supply for chronic pain; no more than 7-day supply for acute pain (with limited exceptions). 3 hours CE every 2 years required for opioid prescribers.

APRN may prescribe opioid controlled drugs classified in schedule II through IV; subsequent evaluation required at intervals appropriate for patient, medical condition, and drug, but not less than annually

Schedule II controlled substances may be prescribed only if patient has terminal condition, physician initially prescribed, and prescription does not exceed 72-hour supply, except in certain healthcare facility settings
prescribing, dispensing or administering opioid drugs in excess of the maximum limits authorized in Section 2-309I of Title 63 of the Oklahoma Statutes
Schedule II narcotic substances limited to five-day supply except for hospice, palliative care, or long-term care facility patients

A nurse practitioner who had been issued a certificate of fitness may only prescribe or issue a Schedule II or III opioid listed on the formulary for a maximum of a non-refillable, thirty-day course of treatment unless specifically approved after consultation with the collaborating physician before the initial issuance of the prescription or dispensing of the medication.

Board must adopt rules establishing requirements for prescribing opioid drugs, including dosing criteria requiring consultation with pain management specialist above certain thresholds; APRNs must inform patients of right to refuse opioid prescription

fields.rationale: States cluster around whether they emphasize equal telehealth/in-person standards, APRN prescribing specifics, patient consent/confidentiality requirements, mandatory in-person visit triggers, delegating rulemaking to the board, or limiting telehealth to collaborative practice contexts.

assignments.raw_value: Advanced practice registered nurses may prescribe non-controlled substances without physical examination if follow-up care is available and records are sent to primary care provider with consent. May prescribe controlled substances under same conditions if complying with opioid limits. Cannot prescribe via internet questionnaire or email without prior provider-patient relationship.
Healthcare professional must establish professional relationship; telemedicine may be used if standard of care does not require in-person encounter

Health-care providers may deliver health-care services by telehealth and telemedicine subject to establishing a provider-patient relationship and meeting standards of appropriate practice; treatment and consultation recommendations delivered by telehealth shall be subject to the same standards of appropriate practice as those in traditional settings
The board shall develop and adopt rules as necessary relating to the practice of nursing in telehealth

A provider delivering health care services via virtual care must at all times act within the scope of the provider's license and according to all applicable laws and rules, including but not limited to this chapter and the Idaho community standard of care. Treatment based solely on a static online questionnaire does not constitute an acceptable standard of care.
Nurses providing telehealth must ensure informed consent of the patient and maintain confidentiality of medical information

Licensees may provide telehealth services within their scope of practice and in accordance with standards of practice; board must adopt rules governing telehealth services including standards and restrictions.

An advanced practice registered nurse (APRN) providing nursing services under a collaborative practice arrangement may provide such services outside the geographic proximity requirements if the collaborating physician and advanced practice registered nurse utilize telehealth. Telehealth providers shall be required to obtain patient consent before telehealth services are initiated and ensure confidentiality of medical information.

APRN may prescribe non-opioid and opioid controlled drugs classified in schedule II through IV by telemedicine after establishing APRN-patient relationship; subsequent in-person evaluation required at intervals appropriate for patient, medical condition, and drug, but not less than annually

An advanced practice registered nurse may perform acts by using equipment that transfers information concerning the medical condition of a patient in this State electronically, telephonically or by fiber optics, including, without limitation, through telehealth, from within or outside this State or the United States.

Advanced practice registered nurses may provide telehealth services in accordance with section 4743.09 of the Revised Code, which establishes standards for telehealth services including that standard of care for telehealth equals standard of care for in-person services

An APRN may perform medical acts via telemedicine and telehealth pursuant to a practice agreement without having to be licensed to practice medicine in this State. An APRN who establishes a nurse-patient relationship solely by means of telemedicine shall adhere to the same standard of care as a licensee employing more traditional in-person medical care. An APRN may not establish a nurse-patient relationship by means of telemedicine for the purpose of prescribing medication when an in-person physical examination is necessary for diagnosis.

An advanced practice registered nurse with a certificate of fitness issued pursuant to this chapter, who provides services in a free clinic or engages in the voluntary provision of healthcare services, may arrange for required personal review of the nurse's charts by a collaborating physician in the office or practice site of the physician or remotely via HIPAA-compliant electronic means rather than at the site of the clinic. An advanced practice registered nurse may arrange for up to ten (10) of the required annual remote site visits by a collaborating physician by HIPAA-compliant electronic

For APRNs, electronic, online, or telephonic evaluation by questionnaire is inadequate for initial patient evaluation except for specific circumstances including abortion medication provision, continuing medication for new patients, and emergency situations

With respect to the established patient, the patient shall visit an in-person health care practitioner within 12 months of using the initial telemedicine service or the telemedicine service shall no longer be available to the patient until an in-person visit is obtained
